There is a speech: ‘Let’s cooperate, let’s provide data, let’s guarantee isonomy, transparency, the fulfillment of norms,” and what we see is something barely translated into concrete actions. We call it a façade of transparency or governance — governance washing. For example, we published a study addressing ads that try to delegitimize the electoral process. Several ads that were explicitly attacking the ballots, saying that there was fraud, software problems, were boosted by third parties, in some cases candidates, and the platform allowed them to circulate. Because it turns into revenue. These are very powerful companies from an economic, political, and geopolitical point of view, with the power to distribute, recommend content, and decide what is allowed and what is not, according to private interests.

GV: Which takes us to another highly politicized issue in Brazil: the regulation of social media. The far-right calls it censorship, while other groups say it’s necessary. With what we’re seeing in this campaign, does it get another angle?

NS: A decisão do STF pela inconstitucionalidade parcial do artigo 19 do Marco Civil, que até então eximia as plataformas de responsabilidade pelo conteúdo publicado por terceiros, trouxe um novo capítulo para a discussão sobre regulação. As plataformas são hoje passíveis de responsabilização no Brasil pelo conteúdo de terceiros, mas a gente não pode pensar em qualquer tipo de regulamentação, sem falar de transparência. Tem normas, tem deveres e uma série de condições para que elas possam operar, e nenhuma norma funciona se nós não tivermos mecanismos para garantir que está sendo cumprida. E, em caso de não cumprimento, aplicar algum tipo de sanção ou de banimento. São empresas privadas tomando decisões de acordo com interesses que conhecemos em parte, mas não sabemos como elas são tomadas, como impactam, se favorecem um lado ou não. Não é censura, proibir conteúdos, nada disso, mas criar regras e colocar essas empresas como parte do debate público, porque elas têm um papel central para o debate público. Nós fizemos dezenas de estudos sobre anúncios fraudulentos que as plataformas deixam circular – conteúdos com fraude, golpes, que querem roubar dados, dinheiro da população, propaganda enganosa. A ideia é fazer com que normas, leis que existem no mundo offline sejam aplicadas às redes sociais reais, para que os usuários estejam em um ambiente seguro. O que nós temos visto é que as redes sociais, as plataformas, as big techs, não são capazes hoje de oferecer um ambiente seguro para os usuários e, em caso de contextos eleitorais, como é o caso do Brasil agora, elas não são capazes de garantir condições de transparência, de conformidade com as normas que o Brasil estabelece.

NS: The Supreme Court ruling about the partial unconstitutionality of Marco Civil’s Article 19, which until recently exempted platforms from being accountable for content published by third parties, brought a new chapter to this discussion. Platforms are now liable to be held responsible for third parties’ content in Brazil, but we cannot talk about regulation without transparency. There are norms, duties, and a series of conditions that must be met for them to operate, and nothing works if we don’t have mechanisms to ensure compliance. And, in case of noncompliance, to apply some form of sanction or ban. These are companies making decisions based on interests that we only know partially; we don't know how they are taken, their impact, or whether they favor one side or not. It’s not about censorship, forbidding content, nothing like that, but creating rules and placing these companies as part of the public debate, because they have a central role in the public discourse. We made dozens of studies about fraudulent ads that platforms allowed to circulate — content with fraud, scams, phishing and money-stealing scams, mischievous advertising. The idea is to make norms and laws that already exist in the offline world be applied to social media, so users can have a safe environment. What we’re seeing is that social media, platforms and big tech, are not capable of offering a safe space for their users and, in case of electoral contexts like Brazil’s now, they are not capable of guaranteeing transparent conditions in conformity with the norms established by Brazil.
GV: And, in a more serious scenario, all these elements that you just pointed out could define an election, change the ruling in a country?

NS: Certamente. Quando nós vemos, por exemplo, gastos de campanhas eleitorais, vemos que as campanhas investem massivamente nas redes sociais. As redes sociais são um termômetro e as orientam enormemente. No portal do TSE, a gente vê esses gastos e estamos falando de cifras de milhões de reais. São investimentos bastante consideráveis. Um grande divisor de águas foi [o escândalo da] Cambridge Analytica, que usou dados de milhões de usuários para manipular eleições e resultados. Já estamos acumulando quase uma década, de um certo consenso de que parte das eleições se jogam nas redes sociais, que podem sim mudar o voto das pessoas, influenciar. Isso se aplicou durante muitas décadas à mídia de maneira geral, e as redes sociais trazem um grau de sofisticação, de refinamento porque o conteúdo é hiperpersonalizado. O que uma pessoa recebe não é o mesmo que outra de outro perfil. É um grau de refinamento e de capacidade de persuasão capaz de mudar a percepções sobre eleições e candidatos.

NS: Certainly. When we see, for example, the costs of a political campaign, we see that they are investing heavily in social media. Social media is a thermometer guiding campaigns. At the electoral court portal, we can see the money spent, and we are talking about millions of reais [Brazil's currency]. These are considerable amounts. A great divider was the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which used data from millions of users to manipulate an election result. We’re already reaching almost a decade of a certain consensus that part of the election is played out on social media, which can indeed change people’s votes and influence them. That was applied for many years to media in general, but with social media it gained a certain sophistication, a refinement, since content is hyper-personalized. What a person gets is not the same as another person with a different profile. Such a level of refinement and persuasive capacity is capable of changing perceptions of elections and candidates.
GV: What does this election in Brazil leave as a lesson?

NS: Vermos plataformas não só como intermediárias, mas como quem decide o que as pessoas vão ver. Elas não são apenas transmissoras de informação, não fazem apenas a mediação. Elas decidem, elas fazem a curadoria, elas usam os nossos dados para isso. E nós não temos a menor ideia de como isso é feito. Eu acho que a gente precisa ter em mente, a partir dessa eleição e de outras experiências também, que esse é um problema global. Estamos falando de eleições no Brasil, mas o que a gente vê é a repetição de problemas que já vimos em eleições passadas, com mais ou menos gravidade. São empresas que atuam de maneira global. A maior parte, empresas americanas, que atuam com interesses privados, em alguns casos, abertamente associada ao governo dos Estados Unidos, com relações amplamente reportadas com líderes do governo americano. E não temos nenhum tipo de fiscalização, de transparência, mundialmente, eficaz.

NS: That we can look at platforms not just as intermediaries, but as those who rule over what people will see. They are not merely transmitting information, just mediating. They are making decisions, curating, using our data for it. And we don’t have the slightest idea of how that is done. I think we need to keep in mind, from this election and other experiences as well, that this is a global issue. We are talking about the election in Brazil, but what we are seeing is the repetition of issues that we’ve already seen in past elections, with more or less seriousness. These are companies operating globally. Most of them are US companies, acting for private interests, with widely reported links to US government leaders. And we don't have any kind of monitoring or transparency globally that is effective.

articles.title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
paras: A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game
Originally published on Global Voices

SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety. A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game. Image by the game's developers, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.

There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar, and DOWN SY I MI. To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.
Stefan Filipovic. Photo used with permission.

A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Stefan Filipovic (SF): We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra, an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo, a game about children with diabetes. We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind. The video game SafeClick (Siguran klik) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SF: While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them. Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations. We wanted to try something different. With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SF: We developed the first playable version of SafeClick. The game is currently awaiting approval by the App Store and Google Play. It is designed for mobile devices, with simple, accessible interactions and visual scenarios. One important decision was to avoid punishing users for mistakes. Instead, the game explains what happened and gives them another chance. We worked closely with educators and parents and used their feedback to make the scenarios easier to understand. We are currently in the phase of arranging mentoring sessions with the mentor assigned to us through the project, with the aim of earning additional opportunities to promote the game and reach as many users as possible.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

SF: Although the game will be published soon, the initial feedback from special education teachers and parents has been highly practical. Special thanks to Jelena Zilic and her children, who provided the first useful in-game test users’ feedback. They helped us see that situations, which are difficult to explain verbally, can become much easier when they are shown visually and practiced through a game. For example, instead of simply telling someone not to respond to a stranger online, SafeClick lets them see the message, decide what to do, and practice blocking and reporting that individual, and reporting the situation to a caregiver. I really believe we managed to turn an abstract topic into something young people can actually practice.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

SF: Before this project, we mostly thought about accessibility as a product and UX (interface) issue. Working on SafeClick made us look at it differently. Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life. Communicate, learn, find information, and be part of your community. If a person cannot understand or safely use digital services, they are left out. We also learned that privacy and accessibility should not be things added at the end of development. They need to be considered from the beginning. That is something we will take with us into our future projects.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SF: The biggest lesson for us was that making something technically simple is actually quite difficult. With commercial products, it is easy to keep adding features. With SafeClick, we had to constantly ask ourselves whether a button, animation, sentence, or screen was really necessary. Our earlier experience with Eureka – Edukativna igra and Lea & Leo helped us understand the value of video games for learning, but SafeClick taught us much more about cognitive accessibility and designing with educators and users in mind.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SF: Our immediate objective is to publish SafeClick, launch it in the media, and inform the wider community about the game’s availability. Looking ahead, we plan to build on this experience to develop a wider portfolio of digital tools tailored for marginalized groups and to continue exploring how games and other digital tools can make learning and participation easier for people who are often left out of mainstream technology. We are open to new collaborations and partnerships.

articles.title: Complementary forces: Why activism needs art to drive action
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: ‘A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention.’
Originally published on Global Voices
An urban art piece called “The Post is fast, it's only the letters that arrive slowly” in front of the main Post Office in Skopje, North Macedonia.

This post is by Nikola Pisarev, an art historian and a pioneer of creative activism in North Macedonia, who serves as the program director at the Contemporary Art Center in Skopje. It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In recent decades, practices that bring art directly into people’s everyday lives have become increasingly common. They may be initiated by artists, activists, informal groups, or citizens who use creative means to draw attention to a problem, express disagreement, or call for change. Public spaces become a place where an action meets an audience, provokes a response, and starts a conversation. This approach, when artistic and creative means are used to press for solutions or encourage social change, is called artistic activism.
The “Monument to Diazepam” raised awareness about overuse of prescription drugs. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

At their core, art and activism have different but complementary roles. Activism seeks to change a situation through strategic planning and advocacy; art, on the other hand, is not pro or against but can move people emotionally.

Art can change how people see and experience a situation. It opens up new perspectives and associations, and its effects are not always immediate or easy to measure. Artistic activism brings these possibilities together: It uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change.

Urban art actions in North Macedonia offer local examples for exploring this approach. Many actions were developed through direct engagement with specific problems, rather than as part of a broader methodology. They began with a desire to point out an injustice, raise a question, or help address a problem.
Urban art action “Fishing for Potholes” in Veles, North Macedonia, which included public performance and distribution of photo and video coverage. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.
What makes artistic activism compelling?

It does not always take a large crowd to draw attention to a problem. A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention even when it is created by a small group — or by a single person. This does not replace the power of mass organizing, but it makes action possible when resources are limited.

Additionally, amid the constant barrage of information, an unusual sculpture, a witty message, or an intervention in public space can interrupt people’s routine scrolling. They may photograph and share the action, extending its reach beyond the place where it took place through social media and communication platforms.
Still, a high number of views does not mean the problem has been solved. Visibility is an opportunity that needs to be connected to the action’s purpose.

Within high-risk or authoritarian contexts, creative action can also give activists greater room to act, even under pressure. Humor, metaphor, and unexpected forms can sometimes make a problem visible without direct confrontation. In some cases, the people behind an action can also remain anonymous. This does not make them immune to pressure: The level of risk depends on the context, the subject, and the way the action is carried out. But a creative form may allow organizers to absorb some of that pressure while keeping the affected community less exposed.

Likewise, a problem hidden in reports, procedures, or individual experiences can remain invisible to the larger public. An artistic action can translate a complex situation into an image, object, or scene that people can readily recognize. This can encourage citizens, experts and decision-makers to discuss the problem and possible solutions. The challenge is to make the message clear without distorting the substance of the issue.

Art also has a way of enduring long after it has disappeared from public space. A scene, symbol, or object can become a story that the media and the public continue to share after the intervention has ended.
The people behind an action do not need to specialize in every aspect of the problem. They do need to understand its core, use reliable information, and listen to those directly affected.

There are countless ways artistic activism can affect a community. It might prompt an immediate response from the authorities, change how people see an issue, or encourage other social actors to get involved.
Immediate response and problem-solving

Satirical plaque, supposedly from the Guinness Book of Records for the “World Record for the Longest Road Construction” for an street in Skopje that laid unfinished for years. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Some actions prompt the authorities to respond quickly. This most often happens with concrete local infrastructure problems: potholes, broken streetlights, faults in water or electricity networks, and smaller environmental issues.

North Macedonia has seen many examples: “The Guinness World Record for the Longest Road Construction”; rubber ducklings placed in the mud at the entrance to a kindergarten in Štip; “fishing” for potholes in Veles; a celebration of the first birthday of a landslide near Kratovo; and the swan lake protest in Orhid. These actions made the situation visible and helped bring about solutions.
However, street art actions can also address wider issues, such as personal data protection, disinformation threats, or corruption.
Changing views and perceptions

Some problems are treated as untouchable, while expert and activist explanations can struggle to reach a wider public. Artistic activism can bridge that gap through the accessibility of an artwork: A simple, readable form can make serious phenomena and policies easier to grasp, encouraging people to question views they may previously have accepted or failed to notice.

Simple Styrofoam fins simulated sharks in the Vardar River in the center of Skopje, next to buildings in the shape of sailing ships made as part of Skopje 2014 project. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Some famous examples of street art activism in North Macedonia include “Sharks in the Vardar River,” which commented on the Skopje 2014 project; “The Eyes of the Trees,” about excessive tree-cutting in Skopje; the “Monument to Diazepam” to raise awareness about overuse of prescription drugs; the Ohrid trout’s speech for St. Nicholas Day; the giant nest carrying a message from birds; and the campaign for the referendum to save GTC, the historic public City Shopping Center in Skopje.
Using different approaches, these actions invited citizens to reconsider their views on public policies and decisions.
Added art warns about the plight of the trees. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.
Encouraging public responses and broader engagement

Some actions aim to provoke responses and mobilize a range of actors. These include not only authorities and institutions, but also professional associations, specialist non-governmental organizations and other groups working on specific issues. At times, such groups may engage less often with the problems citizens face, because communication with communities is limited or because they are reluctant to leave their comfort zones.

The media play an important role in this process. Prompted by an action, they seek answers from different actors. When answers are not forthcoming, pressure grows on those actors to take the problem more seriously. In this way, public attention and media coverage can encourage wider engagement.
A “clean air cabin” ironically offering “fresh mountain air” in the city of Skopje, which suffers from excessive pollution. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Early actions on air pollution in Skopje in 2010 and 2011 are one example. With media support, the group “Urban Art Actions” pressured environmental organizations to take air pollution more seriously.

A similar approach appears in “Bread for All” about poverty; “How Many More Victims?” about cyclist safety in Skopje; and more recent actions on river pollution (featuring a mobile statue of floating feces). In these cases, public pressure helped bring the issues to greater attention among organizations and the wider public.

Some of artistic activism’s effectiveness comes from the way actions are made. Preparation often takes place in a studio or garage. It requires serious effort, but can also be an engaging and creative process. Working this way may help people avoid some of the burnout associated with sustained activism, although it does not remove the pressures that can come with public action.

Another source of artistic activism’s effectiveness — and one reason it is becoming more visible in public communication — is its ability to make a problem difficult to ignore. When that happens, the political cost of inaction can rise. Authorities may begin to view a problem in terms of its potential effect on voters at the next election. If the cost of addressing it is lower than, or comparable to, the possible loss of votes, a response and a solution become more likely.

articles.title: Independent journalism under siege in Georgia
articles.author: Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD)
paras: Need for a unity became urgent in April 2025, after the law on approval of foreign grants
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo by Slava Taukachou on Unsplash

This article by Elli Kostika is an edited version of a longer piece, first published on June 11, 2026, by the non-profit journalism organization Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD). This excerpt is published on Global Voices, with permission under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license. Any use of images or charts by third parties requires permission.

As Georgia has dropped to 135th place in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, iMEdD spoke with representatives of four independent media outlets about the challenges facing journalism in the country: imprisonments, attacks, “foreign agent” laws, and the struggle for survival.
Tamar Rukhadze, Deputy Director of Georgian outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti, describing the state of Georgia’s press, said:

Ι cannot remember any other period in Georgia’s recent history, since I’ve started as a journalist in 1997, with such a harsh and hostile environment towards journalists, media workers and civil society.

Georgia’s government, led by the Georgian Dream party, has intensified its crackdown on media by adopting a series of restrictive laws aimed at suppressing the country’s independent media. Meanwhile, Georgian journalists have been facing constant threats, from legal challenges to physical attacks.

Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding, with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted, opposition politicians jailed, a decline in judicial independence, and a disputed election in October 2024.

Although Georgia has been an EU candidate country since 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream Party, founded by oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, has pivoted the country’s foreign policy towards Russia. However, large segments of Georgia’s population remain pro-EU, and citizens have been protesting for over 500 consecutive days since November 2024, following the contested October 2024 elections and the government’s decision to suspend efforts to advance Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028.
As the struggles of Georgia’s independent journalists have intensified in this increasingly repressive environment, so too has their determination to survive.
A CEO behind bars, yet her colleagues press on

Batumelebi and Netgazeti have paid a heavy price for their independence. The outlets’ co-founder and CEO, Mzia Amaglobeli, was arrested on January 12, 2025, after an altercation with a police chief in Batumi, Georgia’s second-largest city. Following a trial which press freedom groups denounced as politically motivated, Amaglobeli has been sentenced to two years in prison.

In December 2025, the European Parliament awarded her the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. She remains detained under deplorable conditions. Her eyesight — already poor before her imprisonment — is now almost completely lost, Rukhadze tells us, while her lawyers spent six months securing permission for her to visit a clinic, as medical facilities within the penitentiary system lack proper equipment.

In an interview with iMEdD, Rukhadze stresses the deep psychological effects Amaglobeli’s sentence has had on the newsrooms. “We aren’t the same as we were earlier before this imprisonment,” adding, “It’s a nightmare for every single journalist to become news.”
Rather than resorting to self-censorship, Batumelebi’s and Netgazeti’s journalists have persisted in their reporting. She highlights:

The first thing Mzia did after her arrest was to send a message from prison, asking her team to continue their work as before — to do what they had always done and what they are known for: professional, ethical watchdog journalism that gives a voice to those who need it most.

Arrests and detainments are only one of the ways the Georgian government uses legislation against the country’s independent media. Nino Bakradze, co-founder and editor-in-chief of iFact, tells iMEdD they have lost 90 percent of their income since May 2025 owing to a series of laws that have restricted the outlet’s access to foreign funding.

Georgian media, civil society organizations, and individuals receiving financial support from abroad are obligated to register as foreign agents under the 2025 Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and face criminal liability for noncompliance. When such provisions are combined with the 2025 amendments to the law on grants, which require foreign donors to obtain governmental approval before offering grants to Georgian recipients, the causes for iFact’s financial troubles become clear.

Because foreign grants had been a major source of funding for Georgia’s online media for years, as Rukhadze explains, iFact’s financial situation is far from unique. Batumelebi and Netgazeti are also struggling financially: “It’s not about a bright future or expansion or professional growth or anything. It’s about just survival,” Rukhadze stresses.

In March 2026, access to foreign funding was further restricted when the Georgian parliament adopted new amendments to the law on grants, expanding the definition of a “grant.” In 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream government tried to adopt legislation requiring media and civil society organizations that receive over 20 percent of their funding from abroad to register as “foreign agents.”

Although mass protests prevented its immediate adoption, the “Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence,” commonly known as the “Russian law” due to its perceived similarity to Russia’s “foreign agent” law, was passed in May 2024. Batumelebi and Netgazeti have refused to register as foreign agents, Rukhadze tells us, as have most Georgian independent media.

Amid such restricted legal and political circumstances, the trust between sources and journalists has been disrupted. Georgians are now often reluctant to talk to iFact’s journalists and request to speak under anonymity in fear of consequences, explains Bakradze. There have been cases of people who have lost their jobs or access to social aid after openly criticizing the government, she adds.
Attacks, smear campaigns, and surveillance
Since 2023, watchdogs have recorded 65 cases of physical assault and 83 verbal attacks against Georgian reporters.

Sulkhan Meskhidze, who started working as a journalist in 2010, is no stranger to physical and verbal harassment. Such incidents have intensified in the last five years, he tells iMEdD, highlighting that in nearly half of his in-the-field reporting trips, he becomes the target of attacks.

The most serious attack Meskhidze faced came in February 2025, while he was reporting on the deaths of two kids at a public construction site in an area of Batumi called “Dream City.” A group of people began throwing stones at him and demanding that he leave. According to Meskhidze, the aggressors were local residents and government supporters.
The police were present, Meskhidze says, but did nothing to protect him. Even when he managed to record and publish evidence of such attacks, authorities still remained indifferent.

iFact has recently experienced a different type of attack, in the form of smear campaigns. After the outlet published an investigation regarding how Russian oil continues to move through Georgian ports despite international sanctions, the European Commission decided to put Georgia’s Kulevi port on a potential sanctions list. Following that, in March 2026, pro-government media “labeled us as spies of the British intelligence service,” Bakradze explains.

Physical and digital surveillance presents another challenge for iFact. “A lot of the time we see the state security people around us,” Bakradze says. Their phones are also being surveilled and cyberattacks are common.
Survival tactics: From wine tasting to yoga
Bakradze, who co-founded iFact in 2016, tells iMEdD she would not have decided to establish an outlet today.
When you start the week on Monday, you never know if you’ll last until Friday or not.

Since losing their foreign grant revenue, iFact is now relying entirely on local Georgian-derived income, selling a monthly newsletter on sanctions evasion, while also offering a paid membership, the first outlet in Georgia to do so, she says. Events are another revenue source, with iFact organizing a wine tasting event in May 2026.

What has helped iFact’s reporters cope with stress is making themselves busy and seeing the results of their investigations, Bakradze says, adding that “we do yoga as a team.” Sulkhan Meskhidze worries mostly about the stress his family is facing, who live in constant fear for his wellbeing.

Georgia’s independent media have forged a collective response in the form of Sinatle Media, a solidarity and sustainability network of 22 online media. As Sinatle’s Chair of the Board and journalist at the investigative outlet Studio Monitor, Teo Kavtaradze tells iMEdD, the need for a united front became increasingly urgent in April 2025, after the law requiring government approval to obtain foreign grants was adopted. Following a lengthy bureaucratic process, Sinatle Media was born in July 2025. The Georgian journalists who spoke to iMEdD all work for media outlets that belong to the network.

In Georgian, Sinatle means “light.” Both the name and the network’s slogan, “The lights must stay on,” were chosen to underscore a shared conviction: “If the lights go out, the truth disappears with them,” Kavtaradze highlights.

One of Sinatle Media’s main functions involves collecting funds that are allocated to its 22 members. Through a series of events, including book fairs, flea markets, and artwork auctions, Sinatle has managed to raise GEL 260,000 (approximately EUR 84,000).

The network also provides cost-sharing services, which proved particularly valuable in December 2025 during a smear campaign against the network. Sinatle Media helped its members secure legal support to counter these allegations.

One of Sinatle’s main achievements, according to Kavtaradze, is that this is “the first case when we [Georgian media] are actually helping each other […] and we are building this solidarity together.”

articles.title: Unlocking the secrets of the ‘Dragon Man’ skull – and what it reveals about human evolution
articles.author: Chris Stringer, Honorary Professor, Institute of Archaeology, UCL; Natural History Museum
paras: In September 2018, China Daily ran a story that found its way to my desk. It featured the photograph of a beautifully preserved fossil skull with huge brow-ridges, with a caption speculating – wrongly, as it would turn out – that it belonged to a species of human known as Homo heidelbergensis.

The article told a remarkable story about the discovery of this fossil some 85 years earlier. Japanese forces had been occupying the city of Harbin in north-eastern China in 1933. They ordered a team of local workers to help build a railway bridge across the Songhua River.

The workers uncovered the skull in river deposits, and one of them hid it from the Japanese by lowering it down a disused well. Feeling ashamed of having worked for the enemy, he kept quiet about the find for many years. Finally some 80 years later he told his son and grandson as he lay dying, which led to the almost intact skull being recovered and later donated to Hebei Geo University near Beijing.

That origin story is difficult to verify, and there were rumours that the fossil was actually a fake, but I was able to confirm first hand that it was real when I was invited to join Chinese researchers in studying this astonishing relic at the end of 2018. I jumped at this wonderful opportunity to help put one of the most complete human fossils ever found in its proper place in human evolution.

Establishing that place has got a lot trickier in the last 20 years or so. We think that humans (or hominins) split from the ancestors of our closest living relatives, the chimpanzees, about 7 million years ago. For the next 5 million years or so, the hominins continued their evolution in Africa, and about 2 million years ago, began to disperse across Asia and Europe.

It used to be thought that human evolution then progressed from more primitive forms through to modern humans (Homo sapiens), either in just one region, most likely east Africa, or across the whole inhabited world, following the early exit from Africa. Now, we know it wasn’t so simple.

Welcome to our series on the great mysteries of archaeology. Viking explorers, Amazonian cities, artefacts from before civilisation. Archaeology may be all about the past, but it’s constantly shifting with every scientific discovery. This series will dig into some of the most fascinating debates in the field today.

There was a profusion of different kinds of humans, sometimes living at the same time and even in the same regions, as nature conducted multiple experiments over millions of years in how to become human. We are the sole survivors of all those experiments.

Even during the last 300,000 years the number of human species has been startling. The ancient Homo heidelbergensis, with their heavy-set physiques and large faces and jaws, was surviving in Europe – along with similar people in Africa – 300,000 years ago. The even more ancient Homo erectus, which had a smaller brain and angular flat-topped skull, was clinging on in parts of Indonesia until at least 100,000 years ago.

Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthal human), with a broad thick-set body and protruding midface around a large nose, was living in western Eurasia from at least 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. We Homo sapiens – first given that name in 1758, meaning “wise human” – existed at least 300,000 years ago, first in Africa and then globally within the last 50,000 years.

In addition, there are three enigmatic small-bodied forms (and also known to be small-brained in the first two cases) from the same recent period: Homo naledi (star human), Homo floresiensis (Flores human) and Homo luzonensis (Luzon human). These lived respectively in South Africa about 300,000 years ago; on the island of Flores, eastern Indonesia, from at least 190,000 to 50,000 years ago; and on the island of Luzon, the Philippines, about 130,000 years ago. All three seem to be long-lasting relics of even more ancient stages of human evolution.

Our study of the Harbin skull added yet another species to the list. When my Chinese colleagues sent me a full-size 3D print of this skull, I couldn’t believe it. I’ve seen hundreds of fossil human skulls, and this was the biggest I had ever set eyes on.

Our analyses showed it was clearly different from fossils of sapiens, neanderthalensis, heidelbergensis and erectus. It showed a distinctive combination of a very large brain size, a massive brow-ridge and a large, low but rather smooth braincase without the other bony ridges found in erectus and heidelbergensis skulls. It also had a big but modern-looking face with delicate forward-facing cheekbones but very wide nose and large eye sockets.

This warranted a new species name, and in 2021 my Chinese colleagues chose Homo longi, named after the Black Dragon River (Heilongjiang). Ever since, the skull has been known as Dragon Man. It appears that this species was in eastern Asia from at least 300,000 until about 45,000 years ago. All these human timespans are show on the chart below (click to make it bigger).

Not only did the skull turn out to be a new species of ancient human, it also helped to solve several mysteries about other discoveries. One of the keys was its single preserved tooth – a very large second molar, with no sign of a socket behind it for a third molar. In other words, Dragon Man did not have wisdom teeth.

These dental features provided a link with other less complete fossils from China that also had large molars but no wisdom teeth. This and other resemblances indicated that these were also Homo longi, overturning previous possibilities that they might have belonged to an Asian branch of Homo heidelbergensis or an interim species between Homo erectus and modern Asian humans.

It also shed light on the mysterious Denisovans, named after Denisova Cave in the Russian part of the Altai Mountains. Archaeologists had been digging there for decades, finding thousands of animal bones and stone tools, but only scraps of human bones and some large molar teeth.

In 2010 one of those bone scraps – part of a little finger – yielded ancient DNA matching the quality of modern bones. This was despite being about 60,000 years old, showing the astonishing preservation potential of this cold and dry cave in southern Siberia.

Thanks to DNA yielded from other fossils and even sediments from the site, we know the Denisovans occupied the cave intermittently from more than 200,000 until about 45,000 years ago, when Homo sapiens took over.

Placing the Denisovan genome on the human evolutionary tree was difficult, but also in 2010 a high quality Neanderthal genome was reconstructed from European fossils. The Denisovan genome was quite different both to this and to modern humans.

Fast-forward a decade and our analyses suggested that the molars found in Denisova Cave were also from the same species as the Dragon skull. More recently the Harbin skull has been analysed for DNA and fossil proteins, confirming both the connection to Denisova Cave and various other fossils found in China. These include a jawbone from a cave high up on the Tibetan plateau, bones dredged up by fishermen from off the coast of Taiwan, and remains recently described from a cave in the south-west of China.

The skull therefore turns out to be the most complete example of a species that palaeoanthropologists have been circling for some time. It’s now known by both names: Denisovan and the more formal Homo longi.
Having established Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes, it has been possible to compare them with those of people from around the world today. The results have been very surprising.

If people today had evolved from Neanderthals, we might have expected that modern Europeans would show the highest levels of Neanderthal DNA in their genomes, since Europe is where most Neanderthal fossils have been found over the last two centuries. It turns out they do have Neanderthal DNA, at a level of about 2%. But that level of DNA is also found throughout the world today, apart from Africa, where the level is generally much lower.

When similar comparisons were made for Denisovan DNA there were even more surprises. The highest levels were not in modern Siberians or Chinese, but in people from places like the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and Australia – in some cases at levels of around 4%.

How can we explain these unexpected results? Well, we know that the vast majority of our modern human genome – more than 90% – derives from Africa. About 50,000 years ago, having evolved there, the main ancestral wave of early Homo sapiens migrated to western Asia. There they encountered local Neanderthals and did a bit of interbreeding.

That may seem impossible for different species, but today we know from thousands of genome studies that closely related species can often breed hybrids successfully. Examples include jackals and wolves, polar bears and brown bears, and Canada and Greylag geese. It can take millions of years for enough genetic differences to accumulate to make such interbreeding impossible, and that hadn’t happened in the cases of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans.

Those intermixed Homo sapiens in western Asia then spread out to every corner of the world, taking their Neanderthal DNA with them. A lot of it was selected away since it was potentially harmful, causing genetic incompatibilities in regions like the brain and reproductive organs. But other segments were kept as they helped survival, for example protecting against diseases outside of Africa. Over time, the Neanderthal DNA settled down to about the 2% of the modern genome that we see outside of Africa today.

As for the Denisovans, they too interbred with early Homo sapiens groups reaching east Asia. This happened at a lower level in mainland Asia, and seemingly at a much higher level as the Homo sapiens spread across islands of south-east Asia like Borneo and Sulawesi. So far there is no evidence that those other late-surviving relatives such as Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis contributed detectable amounts of their DNA to our genomes today. Either there was no interbreeding, or the species were too different to produce viable hybrids.

We don’t yet have fossil remains from those islands to prove the Denisovans were there before Homo sapiens, only archaeological evidence such as butchered animal bones and stone tools. But assuming this idea is correct, the Denisovans must have been a very successful and adaptable species, surviving freezing winters in northern China but also thriving in tropical grasslands in places like Sumatra. As previously mentioned, they were even living on the Tibetan plateau at altitudes above 3,000 metres.

And by the way, the same Russian cave provides evidence of another dimension to this story. DNA shows that Neanderthals were also there some of the time, and that the two species interbred. We know this from another bone fragment, whose owner, a young girl, was the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and Denisovan father.
What we got right and wrong

Most of what I’ve talked about here, we’ve only learnt in the last 16 years. For my PhD more than 50 years ago I was testing the then widespread idea that modern humans evolved directly from Neanderthals. I spent my time measuring and comparing fossil skulls, using the primitive measuring techniques and limited computing power available at the time.

I concluded that we did not evolve from them. I could see no sign that Neanderthal fossils in Europe were gradually changing towards a more modern anatomy. They weren’t developing a more rounded braincase, a smaller browridge or a more pronounced chin.

Yet now, with genetic powers that I could never have imagined, we can see that my PhD quest only gave part of the answer. Certainly we did not evolve from Neanderthals but yes, they are partly our ancestors because of that ancient interbreeding. Twenty years ago I would have told you that any interbreeding with Neanderthals was trivial in the big picture.

Together with the findings about interbreeding between modern humans and Denisovans, I have to concede that our more recent origins are only mostly out of Africa, not 100%. It means the Neanderthals and Denisovans didn’t die out completely 30,000 or 40,000 years ago: bits of their DNA live on in us today, and some of it is still active.

As for our African beginnings, it was in the 1980s and 1990s that these became clear as DNA sequences from recent human populations accumulated, as well as better fossil material. However, recent evidence suggests that our African origins were quite complex, with several lineages evolving in parallel in different parts of the continent and mixing now and again. For instance, some geneticists think ancient interbreeding with Homo heidelbergensis could have contributed to our evolution, so the human origin story keeps getting more complex.

It’s difficult to imagine what even the next ten years will bring, as work on ancient DNA is developing so fast – along with the newer field of ancient proteomics, which studies fossil proteins. Scientists are turning to these because DNA survival is patchy, especially in warm conditions and deep time.

For example, scientists are looking for traces of the connective tissue collagen, which is widespread in our bodies, skeleton and teeth. Collagen is much more resilient than DNA, and has already been identified in fossils that are millions of years old. As the work progresses and we can sequence the different amino acids in these ancient proteins, we will start to gather knowledge of fossil relationships where DNA cannot reach, as has already been achieved for the Dragon Man fossil.

The fossil record itself will undoubtedly continue to surprise us with unexpected finds, hopefully including eagerly awaited Denisovans from the islands of south-east Asia. Also waiting to be found somewhere are fossils of first-generation hybrids between our species and the Neanderthals, and our species and the Denisovans.

Meanwhile I’m still pursuing the biggest puzzle of them all. Why are we the only surviving species out of dozens that preceded us, and the half-dozen that were still living alongside us 100,000 years ago? Did we overcome them through our better brains or better adaptations or did we just get lucky, time after time, as first the Neanderthals went under, then all the others?

I suspect competition for often limited resources was an important part of the story, where we may have been that bit more efficient than our surviving relatives, but we simply don’t know the full solution yet. More discoveries from archaeology, fossils and DNA will lead us closer to the answers.

articles.title: The Crucible: Arthur Miller’s morality tale was as much a reaction to his own marital failings as it was to the ‘red scare’
articles.author: Jan Machielsen, Reader in Early Modern History, History, Archaeology and Religion, Cardiff University
paras: Written at the height of the cold war “red scare”, Arthur Miller’s 1952 play The Crucible was a retelling of the 17th-century Salem witch trials (1692-93) which soon became the classic parable of mass hysteria.

Miller’s play has long been described as “a cornerstone of American theatre” and “an allegory of our times”. Adapted into a 1996 Oscar-nominated Hollywood film, recent stage revivals on Broadway (2016) and at the UK’s National Theatre (2022) further confirm its enduring popularity.

A staple of the high-school syllabus (a YouTube search yields over 3,200 school productions), the play has also come to shape popular understandings of early modern witchcraft. As Miller (1915-2005) foresaw, its interpretation of Salem became a flexible model applicable to other tragedies – so flexible, in fact, that “witch-hunt” has in recent years devolved into a virtually meaningless political catchphrase.

While acknowledging some artistic licence, Miller still claimed to have captured Salem’s “essential nature”, insisting that “the fate of each character is exactly that of his historical model”. As a work of history, however, The Crucible is deeply flawed; as a morality tale, it can even be described as positively harmful.

The central conflict driving the play – and the witch-hunt – is sparked by the illicit romance between John Proctor, an affluent householder, and his former teenage servant, Abigail Williams. As the witch-hunt unfolds, Abigail – described in the stage instructions as “a strikingly beautiful girl … with an endless capacity for dissembling” – feigns bewitchment and accuses Proctor’s suspicious wife Elizabeth (who had dismissed her from their service) in an apparent bid to take her place.

To save his wife and undermine Abigail’s credibility, Proctor confesses the affair. This gamble, however, spectacularly backfires when Elizabeth perjures herself, denying knowledge of the relationship to save her husband’s reputation – a dramatic twist that legitimises their servant’s accusations and seals their fate.

Notoriously, the Salem court executed only those who maintained their innocence. In the final act, Proctor is offered a reprieve if he confesses to witchcraft, but he dramatically refuses to lie: “How may I live without my name? … I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” With this final defiance, the flawed hero chooses death and redeems himself. To drive that point home, the play concludes with Elizabeth’s absolution: “He have his goodness now.”
In his 1987 autobiography Timebends, Miller described visiting “half-forsaken” Salem himself and going through the records and accounts in its Historical Society building.

“Almost every testimony I had read,” he recalled, “revealed the sexual theme, either open or barely concealed.” He found “hard evidence” of Abigail Williams’s “determination to get Elizabeth murdered”, recognising in one description “the joyous terror of the killer about to strike”. In a 1996 New Yorker article, he maintained again that “John Proctor had bedded Abigail”.

John Proctor was indeed one of the 19 victims of the Salem witch-hunt; Elizabeth survived the panic, her execution at first postponed because of a pregnancy. The real-life Proctor had also been a scathing critic of the court’s use of spectral evidence – the diabolical fits supposedly experienced by the child accusers.

This, however, is where the historical evidence and Miller’s drama diverge. Proctor was in his sixties, not in “his middle thirties”. Abigail Williams is presented as 17 in the play; she is played by a 24-year-old Winona Ryder on screen. Miller acknowledged that “Abigail’s age had been raised” but never stated by how much. Contemporary sources make clear that she was at most 12 years old. There is no evidence she was ever Proctor’s servant, let alone his lover.

All too often, when we study early modern witches, we see ourselves. Miller’s supposed “hard evidence” was little more than personal projection. In Timebends, the playwright admitted that he “had been searching a long time for a tragic hero”. In the New Yorker, he reflected how his own marital failings had caused him to empathise with Proctor:

My own marriage of 12 years was teetering and I knew more than I wished to know about where the blame lay. That John Proctor the sinner might overturn his paralysing personal guilt and become the most forthright voice against the madness around him was a reassurance to me, and, I suppose, an inspiration.
This relatable Proctor did not exist; Miller had invented him.

This points to two ways in which The Crucible is a deeply problematic work of fiction. First, by blaming the Salem tragedy on Abigail Williams, Miller roots a witch-hunt – of all things – in female malice. Second, by constructing Proctor as his hero, the playwright also employs the play and its supposed historic content as a vehicle for his own redemption.

Underpinning both distortions is a refusal to engage with the complexities of history. They show how easy and tempting it is to simply invert the original moral polarity, transforming not only accused witches into saints, but an allegedly bewitched child into a conniving teenage vixen.

Historians now recognise that many of Salem’s young accusers were deeply traumatised survivors of the Indian Wars (1688–1697); some even witnessed the brutal murder of their parents. Abigail, too, was orphaned, though the cause remains unknown.
Attributing blame and responsibility is rarely as straightforward as we would like it to be. Historical research requires careful study of both the evidence and our own biases.

The Crucible does not capture the “essential nature” of the Salem witch-hunt, but it does reveal a great deal about its mid-20th century author – and the anxieties, desires and misogyny that drove him.

“Oh! Bob Marley, right?” Jamaican culture has been popularised by the mainstream, and as a Jamaican-American, I often get a glimpse into how others have consumed it and from what point of view. I would not call myself an ardent Marley fan, but I know the kind of people who are most likely attached to his music outside of Jamaica — for example, the potential counterculture student of the 1970s at UCLA who found connection to his messages of resistance.

My personal fascination with Jamaican music is the “riddim” — the Jamaican patois spelling of “rhythm” — an instrumental beat or tune constructed not for a single artist, but to be used by the collective of the time and to be both enjoyed and critiqued by the culture makers of Jamaican art: the disenfranchised masses.

As a public interest technologist and digital rights advocate, I view the “riddim” with an open-source lens. It helped to protect Jamaican culture, particularly from Western constructs that are heavily embedded in existing power dynamics like rigid copyright laws and the corporate commodification of music.

Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party. In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “Rude Citizenship,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth. Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit.

Beat-sharing directly challenges neo-colonial copyright’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality. Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression, enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky. Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim. If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has.

Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well. I used to watch “passa passa” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s. These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability. The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m.

But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio.
Library of Congress – Banana farming in Jamaica. Fair use.
The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception.

Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind. More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines.

In 1992, the IMF created terms that heavily impacted Jamaica’s economy. This served as the backdrop for the Jamaica Copyright Act of 1993, when the country was directed to reshape its laws to participate in global trade. More rigid terms forced artists to start registering “riddims,” and while these laws are purported to protect artists, less resourced and independent artists struggled to make claims against large producers. This also killed the “handshake agreements” many artists and producers made prior to 1993.
Modern dancehall and beyond
A dancehall party flyer. Photo courtesy of OpenVerse. Public Domain.

This hasn’t stopped dancehall creators from organising alternative circuits of commerce and performance, social intimacy, and communal engagement. Even today, the continuous nature of dancehall works still causes friction with how copyright laws function.

This year, a monumental copyright case was overturned by a U.S. federal judge who named many famous artists in a list of 150, and affected about 2,000 tracks. The plaintiffs, Cleveland “Clevie” Browne and the heirs of Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson, claimed that the “Fish Market” riddim (also known as the “Pocoman Jam riddim”) was the basis and source of the percussion pattern that runs through reggaeton, the now billion-dollar musical genre with origins in the Spanish reggae of Panama brought by Afro-Jamaican migrants, and further magnified by Puerto Rican artists.

However, the logic was denied. As US District Judge André Birotte Jr. said, “Plaintiffs have not clearly identified what copyrighted work contains the allegedly protectable selection and arrangement they seek to enforce.”

The claim failed to take all selections and arrangements mentioned and tie them to one work. But rather, it referenced a collection of works that mirrored parts over time: “That principle is especially significant here. Skidmore cautioned that a plaintiff cannot ‘reconstitut[e] the copyrighted work as a combination of unprotectable elements’ and then claim that those elements are substantially similar because they appear in an accused work, even where the elements are presented in ‘a different aesthetic context.’”

The nature of riddims is a double-edged sword here. Browne and Johnson were deprived of a chance to share in the profits of their creativity that set the groundwork for a whole new genre of music. If this lawsuit had gone in their favour, the logic could potentially have put any new reggaeton artist to this profit-sharing standard, possibly resulting in conditions only well-backed artists like Bad Bunny could afford to accommodate. Such an outcome could have created a disempowering dynamic for new artists. A power structure riddims fought in the first place.

We can all easily hear the main percussion in Puerto Rican reggaeton and Dominican dembow, but copyright’s ears are selectively biased against rhythm — usually favouring money, the artist’s will to attribute credit to where it’s due, and when the tracks were created in the more popular artist’s career. In fact, Black artists are often credited much later for genre-defining work and after lighter-skinned artists have made their money.

Despite the mainstream push away from collective processes, dancehall continues to evolve. What “makes Jamaicans cool” is the layers of understanding that come with what we share. Copyright creates a stamp in time — a piece of “the cool” the mainstream can manage to freeze and sell. Yet, the true cool develops alongside the collective and remains protected by that shared understanding.

articles.title: Venezuela faces a deepening energy crisis as protests grow
articles.author: Gabriela Mesones Rojo
paras: For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life
Originally published on Global Voices

Screenshots of protests in four states in Venezuela (Zulia, Lara, Portuguesa and Falcón) amidst power cuts across the country, taken from the YouTube video by NTN4 “Venezuelans can’t endure power cuts anymore and take to the streets in protest,” published on September, 3, 2026. Fair use.

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

“Yesterday we didn't have electricity for 11 hours. The day before, it was seven,” explains Yanira, a 33-year-old artist and designer who lives with her ailing 73-year-old father in Maracaibo, one of the cities most affected by Venezuela’s electricity rationing. In a region where temperatures remain high throughout much of the year, going without electricity is more than an inconvenience. For her family, the blackouts directly affect their health, work and daily routines.

Across the country, increasingly long and unpredictable blackouts are disrupting work, education, businesses and sleep. In several cities, frustration has spilled into the streets, with residents protesting outages and blocking roads in the darkness.

In August, residents of various cities, including Turmero and Valencia, took to the streets at night to protest the worsening situation. Their demonstrations came as authorities expanded electricity rationing in response to growing pressure on the country’s fragile power grid.

The crisis is particularly severe outside Caracas, where scheduled outages lasting between six and 15 hours a day have been reported in several regions. Authorities have also introduced shorter working hours for some public sector employees, and reached an agreement with shopping malls to reduce electricity consumption.

The government has attributed the worsening shortages in part to the effects of El Niño, which has brought drought and unusually high temperatures to Venezuela. There is also, however, a series of factors worsening the situation, like the major failure at Guri Hydroelectric plant, where one of its turbines — which generated 770MW — collapsed.

The country’s electricity problems long predate the current weather conditions. Venezuela’s power system has suffered from years of underinvestment, poor maintenance and allegations of corruption, resulting in a system that is increasingly unable to meet the country’s electricity needs.
A crisis measured in lost hours

For residents of Maracaibo, one of Venezuela’s largest and most economically important cities, the crisis has become deeply personal. Yanira says she can spend at least six hours a day without electricity. The outages have affected both her livelihood and her mental health.

She has had a hard time finding a job or even working remotely, because blackouts make it difficult to function. She eventually began running small businesses from home, first selling sandwiches and cepillados zulianos — shaved-ice treats popular in the region — but keeping food frozen and drinks cold is a constant challenge when electricity can disappear without warning:
View this post on Instagram

The hardest moments come at night. Without air conditioning, sleeping becomes difficult in Maracaibo’s intense heat — and while opening the windows brings some relief, it also lets tropical insects inside. Yanira says the situation has affected her sleep so severely that she began taking sleeping pills.

Her experience reflects a broader problem. According to Venezuela’s 2025 Living Conditions Survey, only around 10 percent of Venezuelans live without experiencing power outages. For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life.

The blackouts are also taking a toll on local economies. The National Chamber of Commerce reported that 38 percent of businesses had closed during the year, amid the combined effects of the electricity crisis and the country’s broader economic difficulties.

In Puertos de Altagracia which, like Maracaibo, is situated in Zulia state, Sara Hernández works at a company that sells bottled drinking water. Even with access to a generator, keeping the business running during outages is difficult because fuel is not always available. The uncertainty makes planning almost impossible. Electricity can disappear at any moment, and some businesses experience more than one rationing period in a single day.

The consequences extend beyond commerce. In Maracay, in Venezuela’s central region, resident Kellys Gallardo told El País that she receives daily text messages from the state electricity company, Corpoelec, warning her about planned outages, but the messages sometimes arrive only after the power has been cut.

Gallardo, who works at a company that manufactures printer ink cartridges, experiences outages both at work and at home. Her children are also affected when electricity rationing disrupts their schools.
From frustration to protest

As blackouts grow longer and less predictable, anger is becoming increasingly visible in public spaces. Residents who once endured outages quietly are now gathering in the streets, blocking roads and demanding solutions. In cities like Turmero, Valencia, El Tocuyo, Caja Seca, Calabozo, Zaraza and Valle de la Pascua, nighttime protests have highlighted how deeply the electricity crisis has entered everyday life.

The year 2026 saw a significant surge in both the frequency and widespread nature of civil unrest across Venezuela. The Observatorio Venezolano de Conflictividad Social (OVCS) documented upwards of 4,000 protests between January and August, a figure that OVCS coordinator Marco Antonio Ponce noted is triple the amount seen in earlier comparable timeframes. Daily demonstrations averaged 22 in August alone, with persistent electricity blackouts ranking among the public’s primary grievances.

For Venezuelans, the problem is about more than having to sit in the dark. It means businesses losing products and working hours, children having no electricity at school, families struggling to sleep in extreme heat, workers unable to plan their days, and people unable to access healthcare. In the Barquisimeto dialisis unit, for example, a lack of power left 42 kidney patients without treatment.
A problem that has lasted for years

Venezuela’s current electricity emergency echoes its 2019 crisis, when severe drought reduced water levels at the Guri reservoir, the hydroelectric complex that supplies a major share of the country’s electricity. One the most important events of this period was a 6six-day national blackout.

Today’s crisis is unfolding on top of years of deterioration in the electricity system. Venezuela has an installed generation capacity of approximately 30,000 megawatts, but currently produces less than half of that amount. The gap becomes particularly problematic during periods of high demand.

The government recently announced new investments aimed at rebuilding the system. In June, authorities signed an agreement with U.S.-based General Electric to restore 1,000MW of generating capacity over two years, with plans for an additional 5,000MW over the following four years.

Another agreement involving the Tocoma hydroelectric project, which began construction in 2007 but was never completed, was also announced. Authorities say these projects form part of a broader effort to recover Venezuela’s electricity infrastructure.

For residents living through the outages, however, long-term plans offer little immediate relief. In a country where electricity shortages have persisted for years, each new blackout carries the weight of a much longer story: one in which an essential public service has become increasingly unreliable, while residents are left waiting for the lights to come back on.
